I read the image. It has no axis units and no narration, so some of this is interpretation.

1. The animation seems to show how US consumer prices (CPI-U) moved over time compared with a "first check" baseline. The baseline is probably the first payment from an income annuity. The label "Aug 2021, age 80: 100.3%" marks the high point of the line. The small boxes underneath may stand for a series of payments or years. The captions say "ILLUSTRATIVE" and "US only · history, not a forecast."

2. The line starts near the baseline, dips slightly, then climbs to its peak at the Aug 2021 label. It then falls back to the baseline. In frame 1 the line runs on well below the baseline to an "Aug 2026" point. In frames 2 to 6 that later stretch is removed, and the line ends back on the baseline. The last box in the row is dimmed in frames 1 and 2 and full from frame 3 on.

3. The most likely meaning is that prices, or the buying power of a payment, can move well away from the starting level over a long retirement. The gap shows up at a specific age, 80. I can't tell from the image alone what the 100.3% measures. It could be a cumulative price change or the value of a fixed check relative to the first one. The animation also doesn't explain why it removes the Aug 2026 stretch.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that inflation can change what a payout is worth over time. That would make them want to compare a fixed payout with one that adjusts for inflation. As someone about to retire and weighing two payout options, I'd take that as a question to ask, not a conclusion.

5. That takeaway is my own conclusion. The animation never mentions annuities, payout options, or any recommendation. Its captions in fact say it is illustrative history and not a forecast.
